title: Between transparency and trust: identifying key factors in AI system perception
tldr: Conjoint analysis with 315 participants revealed two opposing user clusters: one prioritising explainability and AI certification, the other favouring fairness and reliability, with no uniform attribute preference across the full sample.
problem_and_motivation: Existing research on AI trust attributes examines explainability, reliability, fairness, and certification in isolation, leaving a gap in understanding how users weigh these factors against each other in adoption decisions.
approach: Choice-based conjoint analysis with four attributes (explainability, reliability, AI certification, fairness) presented in 18 forced-choice tasks within a healthcare AI scenario.
Sample of 315 German participants recruited via Prolific, with preregistered study design and hypotheses.
Conventional conjoint analysis on full sample to estimate part-worth utilities and relative importance weights.
Latent class analysis using Gaussian mixture model with two components to identify heterogeneous preference patterns.
Separate logistic regression per cluster to test hypotheses.
Demographic and attitudinal comparisons between clusters using t-tests and chi-square tests.
findings: No significant attribute preferences emerged across the full sample, with all three hypotheses rejected at the aggregate level.
LCA identified two distinct clusters with opposing preferences: Cluster 1 (n=182) favoured explainability and certification; Cluster 2 (n=133) favoured fairness and reliability.
Cluster 1 showed significant positive preferences for explainability (beta=0.145, p<0.001) and AI certification (beta=0.193, p<0.001).
Cluster 2 showed significant positive preferences for fairness (beta=0.409, p<0.001) and reliability (beta=0.137, p=0.019).
Cluster 1 optimal combination (62.4% selection probability): no explainability, high reliability, no AI certificate, limited fairness.
Cluster 2 optimal combination (66.9% selection probability): low explainability, medium reliability, low AI certificate, high fairness.
Cluster 1 reported higher AI acceptance and lower AI fear; Cluster 2 reported lower AI acceptance and higher AI fear, with significant differences on both measures.
Full sample most preferred combination (50.8% probability): no explainability, medium reliability, no AI seal, high fairness.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: Contributes to understanding how users form trust in AI systems by revealing that aggregate-level analyses mask fundamentally opposing user preferences. Demonstrates that two distinct user segments exist with fundamentally different trust-building strategies.
directly_justifies: Two distinct user clusters with opposing preferences for AI trust attributes were identified through latent class analysis.
Cluster 1 prioritised explainability and AI certification while showing negative preference for fairness.
Cluster 2 prioritised fairness and reliability while rejecting explainability and AI certification.
No uniform attribute preference was found across the full sample, contradicting hypothesis of universal reliability preference.
Users comfortable with AI accept moderate reliability when paired with high fairness.
limits: Study limited to a healthcare decision-making scenario; findings may not generalise to other AI application domains.
Sample restricted to German participants and may not represent all potential AI system users.
Abstract attribute presentations may not capture real-world user experiences with AI systems.

limitations: Study limited to a healthcare decision-making scenario; findings may not generalise to other AI application domains.
Sample restricted to German participants recruited via Prolific, restricting cultural representativeness.
Abstract attribute representations may reduce ecological validity compared to real-world AI interactions.
Study measures system choice rather than trust directly, though the two are related but distinct constructs.
AI literacy was not explicitly measured and may mediate observed preference differences between clusters.
remember_this: Conjoint analysis revealed no universal attribute preference; two clusters with opposing trust priorities were identified.
Cluster 1 (n=182) preferred explainability and AI certification; Cluster 2 (n=133) preferred fairness and reliability.
Cluster 2 optimal combination achieved 66.9% selection probability with high fairness and low explainability.
AI-acceptant users accepted moderate reliability when paired with high fairness.
Effective AI integration requires adaptive approaches acknowledging diverse user trust-building strategies.
